title: Risk-weighted ApoB: should some particles count more?
summary: A new score combines ApoB, lipoprotein(a), and triglycerides. Calculate the score and see what the early evidence can—and cannot—tell us.
body_markdown:
An ApoB blood test estimates how many potentially artery-clogging particles are circulating in your blood. But one ApoB-containing particle may not carry the same risk as another. Lipoprotein(a), or Lp(a), makes up a small share of the ApoB count for many people, yet a high Lp(a) result can matter for cardiovascular risk.


That motivates **risk-weighted ApoB** : a research score that gives different weights to ApoB, triglycerides, and Lp(a). The question is whether combining them this way helps identify people likely to have another cardiovascular event after a heart attack or related acute coronary syndrome (ACS).


## What did the ODYSSEY OUTCOMES analysis find?


In a[post hoc analysis of ODYSSEY OUTCOMES](https://eppro01.ativ.me/web/page.php?page=IntHtml&project=AHA26&id=1313) , researchers calculated risk-weighted ApoB for **11,957** participants with all three needed measurements. Everyone had recent ACS and was taking optimized statin therapy; the parent trial randomized participants to alirocumab, a PCSK9 inhibitor, or placebo.


Risk-weighted ApoB improved the C-index modestly, from **0.55 (ApoB or Lp(a) alone) to 0.57** . The authors also reported a larger absolute alirocumab benefit at higher values of the score. That benefit pattern came from exploratory analyses; it does not let this calculator predict what alirocumab would do for an individual reader.

*Panel C from the[AHA 2026 abstract](https://eppro01.ativ.me/web/page.php?page=IntHtml&project=AHA26&id=1313) . The curves are unadjusted and show group-level patterns; they are not predictions for an individual.*


## Does the score add anything in primary prevention?


A separate[UK Biobank analysis presented at AHA 2026](https://eppro01.ativ.me/web/page.php?page=IntHtml&project=AHA26&id=3534) tested the score alongside SCORE2, a cardiovascular risk model. It included **281,974 adults aged 40–69** without cardiovascular disease or diabetes at baseline; **8,613 cardiovascular events** occurred over a median 10 years.


Adding risk-weighted ApoB to SCORE2 raised the model’s AUC by **0.0079** . Adding ApoB, Lp(a), and triglycerides as **three separate inputs** raised it by **0.0078** . The difference between those approaches was not statistically distinguishable. ApoB alone added little in this comparison. The score may be a compact way to carry information from all three markers, but this analysis does not show that the weighting beats simply using the markers separately. Its reported categorical reclassification improvement also had a confidence interval that crossed zero.


*Figure from the[SCORE2 abstract](https://eppro01.ativ.me/web/page.php?page=IntHtml&project=AHA26&id=3534) . Its equation uses triglycerides in mmol/L; the calculator below uses mg/dL with the corresponding coefficient, as printed in the ODYSSEY abstract.*


## Calculate the score


The[published derivation and validation paper](https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf1124) gives the equation with triglycerides in mmol/L. Using mg/dL for triglycerides and rounding the converted coefficient gives:


` Risk-weighted ApoB = 0.736 × ApoB (mg/dL) + 0.132 × triglycerides (mg/dL) + 0.215 × Lp(a) (nmol/L)`


### Calculate the study's risk-weighted apoB score


Enter results from the same blood draw. Lp(a) must be reported in **nmol/L** .


ApoB mg/dL


Triglycerides mg/dL


Lp(a) nmol/L


Enter all three values to see the study-defined score.


This is an exploratory research score. It is not a measured ApoB concentration, a treatment target, or an estimate of your chance of a heart attack. If your Lp(a) result is in mg/dL, do not enter it here; there is no universal conversion to nmol/L.


The result is a **study-defined score** , reported in mg/dL. It is not the ApoB concentration measured by your lab. Existing ApoB treatment targets do not apply to it, and it is not a probability of a heart attack. The Lp(a) input must be in **nmol/L** ; a result reported in mg/dL cannot be converted with one reliable multiplier for everyone.


For an example with ApoB 100 mg/dL, triglycerides 150 mg/dL, and Lp(a) 125 nmol/L, the formula gives **120.3** : 73.6 from ApoB, 19.8 from triglycerides, and 26.9 from Lp(a), after rounding. Those terms illustrate the calculation, not each marker’s independent share of a person’s cardiovascular risk.


## What would make this useful in care?


We would want prospective evidence that calculating this score changes a decision and improves outcomes beyond using the three underlying measurements. The ODYSSEY and SCORE2 analyses studied different populations and endpoints, so their prediction statistics should not be compared as though they came from one head-to-head test.


For now, the practical story is to **measure and understand the underlying biomarkers** . A calculator can make the proposed weighting tangible. It cannot yet assign a treatment target, select a drug, or replace an established cardiovascular risk assessment.
